newsitem.title: CUBA: Oil price rise deals Cuban economy another blow.
newsitem.headline: Oil price rise deals Cuban economy another blow.

text.p: Cuba, economically battered by the loss of Soviet aid and by a U.S. trade embargo, received a new blow when U.S. missile attacks on Iraq last month sent world oil prices soaring.

"This situation hurts us a lot, because the prices of the products we need most go up, and in many cases, we are forced to sell ours at about the same prices," Cuba's deputy Economy Minister Jose Gonzalez said in an interview published in Juventud Rebelde newspaper on Sunday.

In 1989 Soviet tankers carried 13 million metric tons of oil to Cuba from Black Sea ports at preferential prices. Since the Soviet Union's demise in 1991, Cuba has only been able to afford seven million tons of crude bought on the world market.
Cuba had projected oil costs of about $135 a ton in 1996, but over the past month prices had shot up to about $175.
Cuba spends about 40 percent of its hard currency income on oil imports each year and its reserves are at rock bottom.
International lending institutions have refused Cuba long- or medium-term loans, and the Caribbean nation pays up to 20 percent interest on the few short-term loans available to it.
Cuban economists expect that the increase in oil prices will cause a domino effect that will mean higher prices for most of the island's other imports.
Gonzalez predicted that Cuba's economy will grow at a rate of about five percent this year, a recovery from the economic free fall of the early 1990s.

Priority use of imported oil has been reserved for the sugar, nickel and tourist industries. So far this year, private automobile owners have received their gas ration of about four or five gallons only four times, Gonzalez said.
Many Cubans fear that higher oil prices will also mean more power outages.
